Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay ahead of what matters most in clinical practice. I'm glad you're here today, because what we're covering in this episode is one of those topics that can genuinely change the outcome for a patient sitting in your chair right now.

Today we are talking about wet AMD. Specifically, we are talking about recognizing the conversion from dry to wet age-related macular degeneration before vision is lost. And I want to be very clear about something from the start. The window between conversion and irreversible vision loss is narrow. Sometimes it is days. Sometimes it is weeks. And as the optometrist who often sees these patients first, you are the one who can make the difference between a patient who preserves functional vision and one who does not.

So let's get into it.

Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in adults over 50 in the developed world. Most of us know that. We see drusen every single day. We monitor dry AMD patients on a regular basis. But here is the clinical reality that keeps retinal specialists up at night. Approximately ten to fifteen percent of dry AMD patients will convert to the neovascular, or wet, form. And when that conversion happens, the structural damage can begin within days of the onset of choroidal neovascularization. The problem is that many patients do not notice symptoms immediately, or they attribute early distortion to their glasses prescription. And that is exactly where your clinical vigilance becomes the most powerful tool in the room.

Let's start with the clinical presentation, because this is where the story begins.

Your patient is typically over 60, often with a known history of intermediate or advanced dry AMD. They may come in for a routine visit, or they may call your office saying something feels off. The classic symptom is metamorphopsia, that distortion of straight lines, the sense that door frames are bending or text is wavy. Some patients describe a gray or dark spot in their central vision. Others notice that one eye seems blurrier than the other when they cover each eye alternately. And some patients, particularly those with good fellow eye vision, will not notice anything at all until you put an Amsler grid in front of them.

This is why the Amsler grid is not optional for your AMD patients. It is a mandatory part of every visit. And I would argue it should be part of your patient education protocol so they are checking it at home between visits. When a patient with known drusen or pigmentary changes calls you and says the lines on their Amsler grid changed overnight, that is a same-day emergency. Full stop.

Now let's talk about what you are going to find on examination, because this is where the clinical picture gets very specific.

On dilated fundus examination, the signs of wet AMD conversion are distinct if you know what you are looking for. The first thing you may notice is subretinal fluid. This appears as a subtle elevation or blister-like appearance beneath the neurosensory retina in the macular region. The retina may look slightly domed or lifted, and the normal foveal reflex may be absent or distorted. In some cases, you will see a grayish-green subretinal membrane, which is the classic appearance of a classic choroidal neovascular membrane. In other cases, the neovascularization is occult, meaning it is hidden beneath the retinal pigment epithelium, and the fundus appearance may be more subtle.

The second major finding is subretinal or intraretinal hemorrhage. This is often the most visually dramatic sign. You may see a dark red or reddish-black hemorrhage beneath the retina, sometimes with a surrounding halo of fluid. In more advanced cases, the hemorrhage can break through into the vitreous, which is a Valsalva-like presentation that demands immediate referral. Even a small dot of subretinal hemorrhage in the macula of a patient with drusen should be treated as wet AMD until proven otherwise.

The third key finding is a pigment epithelial detachment, or PED. On fundus exam, a PED appears as a smooth, dome-shaped elevation of the retinal pigment epithelium. It can be serous, fibrovascular, or hemorrhagic. A serous PED may look like a subtle orange-yellow blister. A hemorrhagic PED can appear very dark and may be mistaken for a choroidal melanoma if you are not thinking about the clinical context. This is where your differential diagnosis skills become critical.

And this brings us to our next segment, which is OCT. Because if dilated fundus exam is your first line of detection, OCT is your confirmation and your roadmap.

Optical coherence tomography has completely transformed how we detect and manage wet AMD. If you have an OCT in your practice, and I hope you do, this is the moment it earns its place. When you are looking at an OCT scan of a patient converting to wet AMD, there are several findings you need to recognize immediately.

Subretinal fluid appears as a hyporeflective, or dark, space between the outer retinal layers and the retinal pigment epithelium. It is distinct from intraretinal fluid, which appears as cystoid spaces within the retinal layers themselves. Both are abnormal. Both indicate active disease. But subretinal fluid in the context of drusen and pigmentary changes is a red flag for neovascularization.

Intraretinal cysts or cystoid macular edema on OCT in an AMD patient should immediately raise your suspicion for wet conversion. These appear as round or oval hyporeflective spaces within the retinal layers, often in the outer nuclear layer or inner nuclear layer.

A PED on OCT is unmistakable. You will see a dome-shaped elevation of the hyperreflective RPE line, with the space beneath it being either hyporeflective in a serous PED, or heterogeneously reflective in a fibrovascular PED. A fibrovascular PED is particularly important because it often harbors type one choroidal neovascularization beneath the RPE, and it is a strong indicator of active wet AMD.

Double-layer sign is another OCT finding worth knowing. This refers to the presence of a thin hyperreflective layer between the RPE and Bruch's membrane, representing a fibrovascular membrane. It is subtle, but it is significant.

Now, if your OCT shows any of these findings in a patient with known AMD or significant drusen, you are not waiting for the next available retinal appointment. You are calling today.

Let's talk about differential diagnosis, because not every subretinal fluid or hemorrhage is wet AMD, and getting this right matters.

Central serous chorioretinopathy, or CSCR, can look very similar on OCT, with subretinal fluid and sometimes a PED. But CSCR typically affects younger patients, often men in their 30s to 50s, and is associated with stress, corticosteroid use, and type A personality. The OCT in CSCR often shows a single area of subretinal fluid without the drusen burden you would expect in AMD.

Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, or PCV, is a variant of neovascular AMD that is more common in Asian and African American populations. It presents with recurrent serosanguineous detachments and can be distinguished on indocyanine green angiography, which your retinal specialist will perform.

Choroidal melanoma, as I mentioned, can mimic a hemorrhagic PED. The key differentiators are lesion thickness on B-scan ultrasound, the presence of orange pigment on fundus exam, and the clinical context of the patient. When in doubt, refer urgently.

Diabetic macular edema can also cause intraretinal fluid on OCT, but the clinical context of diabetes, the presence of microaneurysms, and the pattern of edema will help you differentiate.

Now let's bring this all together with chairside decision-making and your role in management.

Here is the practical framework. Every AMD patient in your chair gets a dilated fundus exam, an Amsler grid test, and ideally an OCT. If you see drusen with pigmentary changes and no fluid, you are monitoring, educating, and scheduling appropriately based on AREDS2 risk staging. If you see any subretinal fluid, intraretinal fluid, hemorrhage, or a new or changing PED, you are referring urgently to a retinal specialist. Same day or next day. Not next week.

When you make that referral call, be specific. Tell the retinal specialist what you found on OCT. Describe the fluid, the hemorrhage, the PED. Give them the clinical context. A well-communicated referral gets your patient seen faster and treated appropriately.

The treatment for wet AMD is intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy. Agents like ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept, and the newer brolucizumab and faricimab work by blocking vascular endothelial growth factor, which drives the abnormal neovascularization. The evidence is clear. Early treatment preserves vision. Delayed treatment results in permanent structural damage to the photoreceptors and RPE that cannot be reversed.

Your role after the patient begins anti-VEGF treatment is equally important. You are co-managing. You are monitoring visual acuity, Amsler grid performance, and OCT findings between injections. You are watching for complications. You are reinforcing compliance with the injection schedule, because one of the biggest challenges in wet AMD management is patients who stop coming for their injections because they feel better. Vision stability is not the same as cure. The disease is being suppressed, not eliminated.

Document everything. Your OCT findings, your Amsler grid results, your referral communications. This is not just good medicine. It is essential for continuity of care and for your own medicolegal protection.

Here is the bottom line. Wet AMD is a time-sensitive emergency disguised as a routine follow-up visit. Your AMD patients trust you. They come to you regularly. You are often the first person to see the signs of conversion. The OCT findings of subretinal fluid, intraretinal cysts, and fibrovascular PED are your clinical alarm bells. The fundus findings of subretinal hemorrhage and membrane elevation are your visual confirmation. And your response, a same-day urgent referral with clear communication, is what stands between your patient and permanent central vision loss.

Stay vigilant. Stay current. And remember that in optometry, the most powerful thing you can do is catch what others might miss.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. If this episode was useful to you, share it with a colleague, a resident, or anyone in your practice who manages AMD patients. And visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in for more clinical episodes built specifically for eye care professionals like you. Until next time, keep your optics sharp and your patients in focus.

The window between wet AMD conversion and irreversible central vision loss can be days — not weeks. As the optometrist who sees these patients first, your clinical vigilance is the most powerful tool in the room. In this episode of Focus Cast by Focuslinks.in, we break down exactly how to recognize neovascular AMD conversion before permanent photoreceptor damage occurs.

We cover the full clinical picture: the subtle fundus signs of subretinal fluid, subretinal hemorrhage, and pigment epithelial detachment that signal choroidal neovascularization, and the critical OCT findings — hyporeflective subretinal spaces, intraretinal cysts, fibrovascular PED, and the double-layer sign — that demand same-day urgent referral to a retinal specialist.

You will also learn how to confidently navigate the differential diagnosis, distinguishing wet AMD from central serous chorioretinopathy, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, diabetic macular edema, and choroidal melanoma using clinical context, OCT morphology, and patient demographics.

We close with a practical chairside decision-making framework covering AREDS2 risk staging, urgent referral communication, anti-VEGF co-management, and the documentation practices that protect both your patients and your practice.

This episode is built exclusively for licensed optometrists, optometry residents, and clinical eye care practitioners managing AMD patients in active practice.

If you are monitoring dry AMD patients, this episode is essential listening. Early detection saves central vision — and that starts with you.
